thread.title: Apple’s iPhone X failed the famous ‘jam study’ - MarketWatch

author: Alessandra Malito
title: Apple’s iPhone X failed the famous ‘jam study’ - MarketWatch

organizations.name: stern school of business at new york university

text:
MarketWatch photo illustration/Getty Images Apple could learn from a famous 2000 experiment in consumer psychology involving a pot of jam. Apple AAPL is reportedly slowing down production of the iPhone X after lower-than-anticipated demand , and we’re all left to wonder: Where did the company go wrong?
The iPhone X was supposed to mark the iconic phone’s 10th anniversary. Instead, Apple is cutting production from 40 million units to 20 million iPhone X handsets in the first quarter, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal , which cited a person with knowledge of Apple’s production goals.
Apple is usually the leader in branding and messaging, but this time it stumbled, said Tom Meyvis, professor of marketing and coordinator of the Ph.D. program in marketing at Stern School of Business at New York University. Consumers were faced with too many iPhones being released at the same time, and too many variations of the iPhone X, he said. “Consumers eventually adapt to everything, even continuous improvements,” Meyvis said.
Shoppers are dazzled by too many choices
A now-famous study in 2000 by psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper presented consumers in an upmarket store with 23 varieties of jam on one day and just six varieties of jam on another day. Those who sampled the jam were given a $1 off the marked price. Even though more people tried jam at the bigger table, only 3% of people bought jam from that table, while 30% bought jam from the table with the fewer items.
Apple fans know the iPhone will make their life easier and they trust the product will fulfill their expectations. But they’re exhausted by the choice. “Apple customers are not necessarily looking for a specific product to fulfill a specific need, they are simply looking to upgrade,” Meyvis said.
A 2015 study published in the Journal of Consumer Psychology, among others, supports that 2000 jam experiment and the so-called paradox of choice. That study identified four key factors — complexity of choice, decision making difficulties, preference uncertainty, and decision goals — that lead to an overload of choice. “We further show that each of these four factors has a reliable and significant impact,” it said.

Apple’s marketing problems with the iPhone X were complex
Apple had other issues making it more difficult for consumers to choose the iPhone X. The iPhone X came out in November 2017 only two months after the Cupertino, Calif.-based tech giant released the iPhone 8 and iPhone 8 Plus. Many people didn’t know what to call the iPhone X when it first came out. (It’s pronounced “10” rather than “X” in honor of the iPhone’s 10th anniversary.)
And they were compounded by trust issues. At the same time as the phone’s release, Apple was in the middle of a scandal, with customers complaining the company for purposefully slowing down iPhones with older batteries to avoid them shutting down. Apple later apologized and dropped the price of replacement batteries from $79 to $29 .
Of course, it’s easier to taste a different jam than figure out how a $1,000 iPhone X is different from the last. The phone has flashy new features, like facial recognition and wireless charging, but experts say the company may be pushing its luck by asking customers to spend so much.
But Apple has built a community of loyal fans, and it’s expanding, said Barbara Kahn, professor of marketing at The Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. People often go to Apple’s stores just to try the products and hang out. “When I’m walking around malls, the Apple store is still the most crowded,” she said. “People are waiting outside on line for the Apple store to open.”
